aions_core/server/generator_cbms.py: This file builds structured answers by combining knowledge base chunks with question context. When someone asks a question, it retrieves relevant text passages from a chunked knowledge management system (CBMS), then formats them into a readable response that includes key points, conversation history, and performance metrics from a ranking system called CRLA. The main function takes a query and several optional inputs like retrieved chunk identifiers, conversation history, and ranking results, then outputs a formatted text string with numbered key points, optional context snippets, performance statistics, and source attribution. It talks to the CBMS system to fetch actual chunk content by identifier, and pulls scoring data from a CRLA ranking system. Someone would ask about this when they need to take search results and turn them into a polished answer with proper citations.
aions_core/server/hangul_addressing.py: This file converts data into Korean Hangul characters for use as compact identifiers or addressing codes. It takes any text input, creates a SHA1 hash of it, and translates that hash into a sequence of Hangul syllables as a way to represent the data. The process involves converting each hexadecimal digit from the hash into a Korean character by calculating an offset from the base Hangul syllable. The main function accepts text and a length parameter, returning a string of Korean characters that uniquely represents the input. It uses only Python's built-in hashlib and character encoding, requiring no external dependencies. Someone would use this when they need a human-readable but compact way to reference data or create short codes for items in a system that supports Korean text.
aions_core/server/korean_keys.py: This file creates searchable matching keys from text by extracting syllable-like patterns inspired by Korean writing conventions. When given a text input, it extracts all word tokens (alphanumeric sequences), then generates two types of key patterns: three-character substrings from the tokens themselves, and three-character groups extracted from SHA1 hashes of the tokens. Each key is prefixed with 'g:' for grammar-based keys or 'h:' for hash-based keys to distinguish the source. The function returns a set of all these keys for rapid matching against query keys. It talks to hashlib for cryptographic hashing and uses regex for token extraction. Someone would ask about this when they need fast approximate matching between search queries and text, or when building a search index that doesn't require exact keyword matching.
control_plane/skills/__init__.py: This is a package marker file that declares the skills module as part of the AIONS Skill Engine. It contains only a single docstring describing the module's purpose for unified object and skill management. The file serves to make Python treat the directory as an importable package with no additional runtime initialization needed.
control_plane/skills/stats.py: This file tracks how well automated skills or tasks perform over time by recording success rates, execution speed, and calculated confidence scores. Each skill gets performance statistics stored in JSON, with counts of successful and failed attempts, average execution time in milliseconds, a calculated success rate percentage, and a blended confidence score that weighs reliability against speed. The confidence calculation prioritizes reliability by default but can be adjusted to prefer speed instead via a preference parameter. Data is stored persistently in a JSON file under the runtime directory, loaded on demand and saved after each recorded execution. It talks to Python's pathlib and json modules to manage file storage. Someone would ask about this when they need to pick between multiple ways to solve a problem and want to choose the fastest reliable one, or when tracking whether automated systems are working well.
mcpServers/VS_CODE_MCP_CODEX/src/patched: This file fixes a Windows buffering bug in MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers that causes multiple JSON-RPC messages to get batched together when they should arrive separately. The server creates an async transport layer over standard input and output that reads incoming messages line-by-line and writes outgoing messages with explicit flush and small delays to prevent bundling. Two background tasks run continuously: one reads messages from stdin and converts them to MCP session messages, the other takes session messages from a write queue and sends them to stdout with a deliberate small pause between messages. It uses anyio for async I/O and the mcp library for message parsing and serialization. Someone would need this when running an MCP server on Windows and finding that Claude receives multiple tool responses as a single batch instead of individually.
This is a comprehensive MCP server that provides Claude with access to the host computer's tools and data. It integrates file searching through Windows Everything or Linux indexing, Docker and container management, WSL Linux distribution control, Git version control commands, network diagnostics like ping, a file scanner that analyzes project structure and dependencies, conversation logging with automatic batching to ChromaDB and JSON logs, memory storage and retrieval through vector search or Korean-key matching, CBMS knowledge base chunk retrieval, Google Calendar event reading, and system health monitoring. Each tool call gets automatically logged to a buffer that dumps when full, creating an immutable record of what Claude tried to do. The server discovers tools like Docker and Git from the system PATH or common installation locations, uses configuration from environment variables for features like HTTP vs embedded vector database backends and search paths, and provides context guards that compress large responses into references to save Claude's token budget. It talks to dozens of external systems including the local filesystem via Everything.exe or Linux indices, Docker daemon, Git repositories, WSL distributions, the operating system for shell commands, ChromaDB for vector storage, CBMS for semantic chunk retrieval, Google Calendar API for events, and the mcp library for protocol handling. Someone would ask about this when they need Claude to interact with their computer's files, run commands in containers, check Git history, search the disk quickly, or store and recall important context across sessions.
server/store_selector.py: This file automatically chooses which vector database backend to use—HTTP or embedded—based on environment configuration or automatic detection. If the CHROMA_USE_HTTP environment variable is explicitly set to 'true', it loads the HTTP implementation; if set to 'false', it loads the embedded implementation; otherwise it tries to connect to an HTTP ChromaDB server by making a heartbeat call to test availability, falling back to embedded if that fails. The file re-exports the VectorStore class and get_connection_mode function from whichever backend was selected. It takes no input data directly but reads environment variables CHROMA_USE_HTTP, CHROMA_HOST, and CHROMA_PORT. The output is transparently swapped imports so the rest of the application always imports from this module regardless of which backend is active. It talks to the chromadb library to test HTTP connectivity. Someone would ask about this when they want their application to automatically work with either a remote shared ChromaDB server or a local copy depending on what's available.
